title: Adaptive Paper: Kumon Economics, AI Back Office
one_liner: Weekly personalized paper practice packets sequenced from phone photos of last week's handwritten work: adaptivity with no screen and no chatbot in the child's hands.
customer: Homeschool and hybrid families (parent pays; ESA/scholarship-eligible later), microschools, Catholic and independent schools, and eventually districts in AI-pause cities.
problem: 61% of teachers want less device use, NYC and LAUSD paused AI, and proctored math performance is sliding while screen-based practice looks better. Adaptive practice has lived on screens where AI can do it for the child. Kumon proves parents pay roughly $100-150 a month for paper mastery, but it is rigid and franchise-priced.
solution: A parent photographs the completed worksheet. The back office reads the handwriting, classifies error types (graphing and hand-drawn work are hard to outsource to AI), and prints or mails the next week's 5-day packet with a one-page parent guide. The student never touches a screen or chatbot. Start with math grades 3-8.
why_now: Handwritten-math recognition from phone photos only recently became reliable and cheap. Screen fatigue and AI bans are mainstream. ESA and scholarship-credit money arrives in 2027, and homeschool ESA families want low-cost vendors.
revenue_model: $15-25 per child per month for print-and-mail, $8 for PDF-only. School licenses of $6 per student per month. ESA-vendor listing to capture ESA dollars.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone equates personalization with screens, but the personalization is in the sequencing, and sequencing can happen off-screen once handwriting is machine-readable. Paper is the AI-proof delivery channel and screens are the liability.
first_30_days: Recruit 40 homeschool families through co-op groups with a $9 first month. Run one grade band of math. Have a retired teacher audit the sequencing weekly. Use a print-on-demand vendor. Measure with a short proctored pre/post check so you have outcome data to sell schools.

title: The 3 A.M. Pharmacist Desk for Konbini
one_liner: A neutral, multilingual, 24-hour remote pharmacist service that issues the emailed certificate the new law will require before konbini without pharmacists can sell OTC drugs.
customer: Convenience-store owners, first independents and multi-chain franchisees in tourist and nightlife areas of Osaka such as Namba, Dotonbori, Shinsekai and Umeda, then chains. Hotels and hostels are a second channel. Stores pay per certificate, or by sharing the margin on OTC sales.
problem: After 11pm, people keep coming in asking for painkillers, stomach medicine, cold medicine, motion-sickness pills, period-pain relief and allergy tablets. Most Type 2 OTC drugs can only be sold when a registered seller is on the premises, and night staff do not have that license. I turn away a steady stream of tourists and night workers every night. Foreign visitors cannot get counseling in their own language even when a pharmacy is open. That is lost margin and a real public-health gap.
solution: Customers scan a QR code on the shelf, choose products, and join a 60-90 second video or chat consultation in Japanese, English, Chinese, Korean or Vietnamese with a licensed pharmacist. They receive a certificate by email or app, and the clerk verifies it on a phone-based web page before ringing up the sale. The pharmacist network is staffed by night-capable remote pharmacists, such as parents and retirees working from home. The operator holds the pharmacy license and takes on regulatory and liability responsibility. Pre-2027, the same desk runs a limited service on quasi-drugs and pharmacy-hours referral lists so the network and the store workflow are ready when the rule takes effect.
why_now: The amended Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Act passed in May 2025. It allows convenience stores without pharmacists or registered sellers to sell OTC drugs after the buyer gets an online pharmacist explanation and an emailed certificate. It takes effect around spring 2027. Lawson has said it plans OTC delivery at stores without pharmacists starting in 2026. Inbound tourism to Osaka remains at record levels. The window for a neutral operator is the next 6-9 months, before chains sign exclusive deals.
revenue_model: ¥300-500 per certificate paid by the store, or 25-30% of the OTC gross margin. Hotels and hostels pay a subscription for guest access. Later revenue comes from manufacturers paying for education and sampling inside consultations, and from chains licensing the network.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for konbini OTC is not shelf space, POS integration or the law. It is a supply of licensed humans awake at 3 a.m., speaking Vietnamese or Chinese, who can explain a drug in 90 seconds. Chains will assume they can build this in-house, but they lack pharmacist labor and multilingual night coverage. A neutral network that any owner can join in an afternoon has the advantage, because independent and multi-chain owners have no other option.
first_30_days: Partner with one licensed Osaka pharmacy, or set up the pharmacy entity, and recruit 10-15 remote pharmacists for night and weekend slots. Build the QR, video, certificate and clerk-verification flow as a web app, tested at my three stores on quasi-drugs and referral flow. Pre-sign letters of intent with 10 owners for spring 2027 pricing. Approach two hotels near Namba for guest access. Meet the health-center pharmacy inspection office to confirm the compliance path before launch.

title: Tele-Drive Home for Retirement Golf Carts
one_liner: A designated-driver and remote-driving service for owner-owned golf carts in age-restricted communities, starting with humans and automating later.
customer: Residents 75+ in golf-cart towns such as The Villages, Sun City and Del Webb communities, and their adult children. Secondary payers are HOAs and developers and restaurants near town squares.
problem: In these communities the golf cart is an 80-year-old's car, with no DMV, no Uber and no bus. Crashes and cart DUIs are a recurring local news story. Families dread taking the cart away, so there is no middle path between 'keep driving' and 'lose independence'.
solution: Phase 1 (start now): a human 'ride-home' service. A driver takes the resident's own cart home and a chase driver collects them, at $15 per ride around town squares and restaurants. Phase 2: a $39-59/month Guardian retrofit for the most common cart platforms, with geofence, speed governor, breathalyzer or quick cognitive-check lockout, crash and fall alerts, and family notification. Phase 3: a 'take me home' button that lets a remote operator drive the cart home at 5-8 mph over private cart paths.
why_now: Remote-operations stacks (cheap cameras, LTE/5G, teleop tooling) are mature at low speeds. Incumbents left a gap: Voyage held a license at The Villages but was folded into Cruise, and Carteav sells whole new autonomous carts to resorts, communities and campuses rather than upgrading the carts residents already own. Insurers and HOAs are hunting for older-driver risk reductions.
revenue_model: Per-ride fees ($10-15). Monthly Guardian subscription ($39-59). HOA or developer sponsorship and restaurant partnerships. Later, insurer discounts or revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The real competitor isn't Waymo but 'no transportation'. Making driving safer instead of ending it protects dignity, which is the emotional job families are hiring for. Low speeds on private paths are where teleoperation is technically and legally tractable today, and a human-run version proves demand and maps every route before any hardware ships.
first_30_days: Embed in one community for a month. Run Friday and Saturday evening 'ride-home' service near town squares at $15 per ride and log every route and ride. Sign 20 families onto a pilot alert package. Pitch sponsorship to local restaurants and the HOA or district. Bench-test a governor, geofence and lockout kit on two carts.

title: Compute-Heated Pools and Saunas
one_liner: Install small immersion-cooled compute clusters in municipal pools, Ys and recovery studios so the servers pay for the heat.
customer: Municipal pools, YMCAs and hotels with heavy heating bills, recovery studios with saunas, and the AI batch-inference buyers who rent the compute.
problem: Pools and sauna rooms are among the largest energy line items in public and wellness facilities and many public pools are cut when budgets tighten, while AI compute needs cooling and dumps its waste heat.
solution: Deploy a 20-50 kW 'digital boiler' in the plant room that heats pool or sauna water through a heat exchanger, sell the compute to latency-tolerant inference or batch customers, and give the facility free or discounted heat. First product: a single-site pilot funded by a state energy grant and reserved compute.
why_now: A UK pilot at Exmouth Leisure Centre (a 28 kW cluster) reportedly cut the pool's gas use by 62 percent and saved about 24,000 dollars a year while the operator paid for the electricity; AI compute scarcity and edge inference demand are high in 2026 and decarbonization grants are available.
revenue_model: Compute revenue shared with the host, monthly heat fee or discount, and grants; gross margin from selling the heat.
non_obvious_insight: Both sides get paid: the compute buyer gets free cooling and the pool gets free heat, and a pool is a 24/7 constant heat sink unlike offices. The real customer is the compute buyer, with pools as cheap distributed real estate. Capital needs are real, so lead with a grant-funded pilot.
first_30_days: Find a gas-heated pool operator and a champion on the board, sign an MOU, commission a 10-20 kW pilot design with an immersion-cooling vendor, apply to two energy grant programs, and pre-sell reserved compute to two batch-inference customers.

title: Fiduciary Collection Executor for Heirs
one_liner: A service that inventories, appraises and sells inherited card, comic, toy and coin collections for estate lawyers and executors, with an audit trail built for fiduciary liability.
customer: Probate and estate attorneys, trust officers, professional fiduciaries and family executors, billed per estate.
problem: Collections built by boomers and Gen X now carry five- to seven-figure values after record card prices, but heirs have no idea what they hold. 'We buy collections' buyers lowball, and executors are liable if they sell below fair value. Large estates and donations also need qualified appraisals.
solution: Photo-inventory intake (on-site or shipped kit), visual identification and comps, graded-versus-raw triage, sign-off by a qualified appraiser, and sale through the best channel (auction house, game store, streaming seller) under a published fee schedule. The output is an estate-ready valuation report with full custody and sale documentation.
why_now: Card prices are at records ($16.5M for a PSA 10 Pikachu Illustrator, $1.4M for a PSA 9). Visual AI has cut cataloging cost sharply. The wealth transfer is under way.
revenue_model: A flat inventory and appraisal fee ($500-3,000) plus a 10-15% sale commission. Referral relationships with law firms.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not the collector but the fiduciary, who carries legal liability. Liability aversion unlocks budget, and the moat is trust artifacts (documented process, appraisal compliance) that any dealer cannot offer because the dealer sits on the other side of the trade.
first_30_days: Give a talk to 15 probate attorneys and 5 fiduciaries in one metro titled 'What is in Grandpa's basement.' Offer a $299 rapid triage, partner with a certified appraiser, and close the first 5 estates.

title: Timed Slots for Viral Fields and Harvest Rescue
one_liner: Ticketing built around bloom and ripeness windows that turns crop-trampling influencers and crew-short fields into capped, paid visitor days.
customer: Specialty and mid-size growers with photogenic or U-pick crops near metros (tulips, lavender, sunflowers, blueberries, peaches, apples, pumpkins), especially those with unharvested acres from crew shortages. Rural tourism boards are a second payer.
problem: Viral fields get trampled while farmers earn nothing, and destinations lack allocation tools (Fuji's hard cap is the model). Meanwhile fruit rotted in fields in 2025 for lack of pickers and late or absent H-2A crews mean lost revenue. Farms squeezed by diesel up 80% and a fourth loss-making row-crop year need any extra income.
solution: Bloom and ripeness forecasts from degree-day models and owner photos drive timed-entry capacity by field zone, waivers, weigh-station POS for pay-per-pound U-pick, and parking and shuttle management. A 'harvest rescue weekend' feature lets a farm that is short of pickers list a paid visitor-harvest event 5-10 days out, with dynamic pricing by forecast and weather. Dispersal nudges route overflow to lesser-known partner farms, and nearby motel beds can be bundled.
why_now: Crew shortages, high input costs and social-media virality are all at peak in 2026, and destinations from Barcelona to Glasgow are moving from fees to allocation. Agritourism liability laws are widespread. Lead times are shortening to about 33 days, so last-minute local trips are growing.
revenue_model: 8-12% of ticket value plus $1.50-$2.50 per ticket in payments. $199/season SaaS for farms. Sponsored dispersal campaigns from tourism boards.
non_obvious_insight: A crop calendar is a supply curve with a 7-14 day peak, so the same forecast tells a farmer when to harvest and a tourist when to come. One dataset prices both the labour gap and the crowd, and U-pick as an emergency labour substitute is a hedge farms already improvise but nobody productises.
first_30_days: Sign 5 orchards and pumpkin farms for immediate October weekend slots to test capacity caps and pricing this month. Then sign 10 farms for spring 2027 tulips and strawberries starting in January, using white-label Stripe ticket pages before building custom software.

title: Vape Amnesty: Hazmat Pickup Funds Teen Quitting
one_liner: Turn the disposable vape from a fire-prone hazmat problem into the top of a cessation funnel: collect vapes at schools and clinics, send the lithium cells to domestic black-mass buyers, and enroll every person who drops one off in a paid quit program.
customer: School districts and county health departments (using youth-vaping settlement and tobacco-prevention funds), plus health plans, Medicaid programs and state quitlines that pay per enrolled quit attempt. Haulers, MRFs and their insurers are a secondary payer for fire-risk reduction.
problem: Vapes are a named driver of the 2026 battery-fire surge: 74 catastrophic facility fires (over $400K each) year to date versus 71 in all of 2024, and one UK hauler saw about 480,000 vapes in two months. Schools confiscate them by the bucket and either pay for hazmat pickup or bin them (nicotine e-liquid can classify as acute hazardous waste in many states, and the cells are Li-ion). Meanwhile cessation programs cannot find teen and young-adult vapers, who do not self-identify.
solution: A 'drop, quit, ship' kit. Fire-rated locking drop boxes sit in school nurse offices, pharmacies, urgent cares and campus clinics. Each box has a QR code that opens a confidential text-based quit coach, with a telehealth clinician for pharmacotherapy where the user is old enough. A licensed universal-waste hauler batches the vapes, discharges and extracts the cells for black-mass sale, and manifests the e-liquid. Districts get a compliance report and an 'alternative to suspension' curriculum. Public health gets anonymized data on which illicit brands and flavors are turning up.
why_now: The Aug 27, 2026 BIS rule forces black mass to be sold to US buyers, so recovered cells have a guaranteed domestic outlet. Battery-fire counts are at 10-year highs and nobody has decided who pays for the losses. California just expanded battery EPR (SB 501). Youth-vaping settlement money is still being allocated by states and districts.
revenue_model: Per-school or per-clinic annual fee for boxes, pickups and compliance reporting ($1-3K per site). A bounty per enrolled quit attempt from plans and state programs. A small hauler and insurer sponsorship for avoided fire exposure. Black-mass proceeds are trivial (a tonne is roughly 50-100K vapes), so the business runs on the public-health and hazmat budgets, not on the materials.
non_obvious_insight: Two budgets that never talk to each other, public health (which pays for quits but cannot find the user) and waste operations (which finds the user's object but only sees a hazard), both pay to touch the same physical item. A vape in a drop box is a self-identified nicotine-dependent person at peak motivation.
first_30_days: Pitch 3 school districts and 1 county health department on a free 'amnesty week' at two high schools. Buy 10 fire-rated collection containers and sign a licensed universal-waste hauler. White-label an existing text-quit vendor. Collect the first ~200 vapes, count flavors and brands, and publish a one-page fire-risk and quit-enrollment report to convert the pilots into paid annual contracts.

title: 30-Day Capacity-Window Plan After Early Alzheimer's Diagnosis
one_liner: A productized sprint that uses the legally competent window after an early blood-test diagnosis to lock down legal, financial, safety and care plans.
customer: Newly diagnosed patients and their spouses or adult children, reached through memory clinics, neurology and primary-care practices, blood-test labs and elder-law firms. Employers with caregiver benefits are a secondary buyer.
problem: Blood tests cleared in 2025 mean many people learn they're on the path to dementia while still competent, with a 3-7 year window to sign POAs, choose agents, set financial guardrails, plan driving and firearm safety, decide on Leqembi and record wishes. After capacity is lost, it becomes a court fight. CMS GUIDE closed enrollment after one 2024 window, so nobody owns the first 30 days.
solution: A fixed-fee, nurse-navigator-led sprint: a capacity-timed legal package via partner attorneys (POAs, directives, HIPAA releases, updated will or trust), financial guardrails (bill-pay automation, bank trusted-contact, scam locks), a safety plan (driving, firearms, stove, wandering), a care roadmap with cost projections and a Leqembi decision aid, and 90 days of dyad coaching.
why_now: FDA cleared Lumipulse pTau217 in May 2025 and a second primary-care blood test in Oct 2025. Leqembi Q1 sales rose 74% to $168M and it now has an at-home subcutaneous starting dose. Diagnosis is decentralizing while post-diagnosis coordination is not.
revenue_model: $1,500-3,500 fixed family fee, plus employer or LTC-insurer contracts. No referral payments from providers, to stay clear of anti-kickback issues.
non_obvious_insight: Earlier diagnosis is a legal-capacity clock, not just a medical event. The valuable window is the one when the patient can still sign, and every document signed in it prevents a $5-15k guardianship later.
first_30_days: Partner with two memory clinics and three elder-law firms, and deliver five pilot sprints at $1,500 each. Track documents executed while competent and family satisfaction.

title: True Pop: De-duplicated Card Scarcity Data
one_liner: A data product that uses image matching to remove crack-and-resubmit double counts from graded-card population reports, showing lenders and dealers how many physical copies actually exist.
customer: Lenders and financiers that take graded cards as collateral, high-end dealers and auction houses, investment-minded collector groups, and insurers pricing slabs.
problem: Population reports count submissions, not unique cards. A card that is cracked and resubmitted is counted twice unless the owner mails back the slip, which most do not. Yet prices, loans and low-pop premiums key off those numbers. With a roughly 12x price gap between PSA 10 and PSA 9 at the top, the incentive to resubmit is enormous, so the most valuable cards are the most double-counted.
solution: For the top ~500 cards by value, ingest public cert-lookup images and sale photos and compute surface fingerprints (print defects, edge whitening, dings) to link cert numbers that are the same physical card. Publish a True Pop and a scarcity-adjusted price index, then add cert-duplicate alerts for buyers at purchase time.
why_now: A PSA 10 Pikachu Illustrator sold for $16.5M in Feb 2026, and cards are now used as loan collateral. Vision models make surface matching cheap. The pop report is treated as truth precisely as the money grows.
revenue_model: API and subscriptions of $300-2,000/month for lenders and dealers, $9 per-card reports for collectors, and data licensing to marketplaces.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone treats the pop report as the scarcity ground truth, so scarcity is systematically mispriced in one direction, and it is worst exactly where the dollars are. The wedge is a corrected number that lenders can underwrite against.
first_30_days: Hand-verify duplicates on 200 high-value cards using public cert pages. Publish a free weekly True Pop on X and Reddit for reach. Sell 3 pilot reports at $500 to dealers or lenders and interview 5 lenders. Get legal review of scraping and terms of use first, and use only public or user-submitted data.

title: Sundowning Night Companion Speaking in Family's Voice
one_liner: A bedside device that detects night waking and reorients a person with dementia in a voice they consented to, escalating to a caregiver or remote night aide.
customer: Family caregivers of people with moderate dementia at home (about 15% provide 60+ hours a week), memory-care communities with thin night ratios, and home-care agencies with overnight cases.
problem: Night waking is a top reason families place a loved one. Overnight aides cost $300-450 a night, and families otherwise absorb 3 am crises. Generic AI companions are seen as deceptive or are not built for dementia.
solution: A bedside speaker or tablet with radar or audio wake detection plays short, clinically scripted reorientation lines in a familiar voice (for example a spouse or child), seeded by a 'voice will' the person records and approves while they still have capacity. It escalates to the caregiver's phone with two-way voice, then to a paid remote night aide, and logs sleep patterns for the neurologist. Guardrails: no impersonation of the deceased, and clinician sign-off.
why_now: Voice cloning from seconds of audio and on-device speech models are cheap in 2026. NY, FL and NJ are giving away ElliQ, showing public payers buy companionship tech, and 23% of 65+ now use ChatGPT, so acceptance is rising.
revenue_model: $199 hardware plus $39-59 a month for families, $30-50 per bed per month for memory care, and remote night-aide add-on fees.
non_obvious_insight: Ethics is the product: an advance 'voice will' turns a controversial deception into a consented comfort, like an advance directive for how you want to be soothed. Night is the least automated and most expensive shift.
first_30_days: Build on a commodity smart speaker with scripted lines, recruit 10 families through Alzheimer's support groups and one neurologist, and measure night-waking events over four weeks. Convene a geriatric psychiatrist and an ethicist as advisors.

title: Inheriting the Lease: Rent-Stabilized Succession Service
one_liner: A service that helps families of rent-regulated elders build and keep the co-residency evidence that lets them inherit a below-market lease, and files the succession claim within days of a death.
customer: Adult children and relatives living with rent-stabilized or rent-controlled elders (about 1M stabilized units in NYC alone, plus SF, LA, Newark and DC). Elder-law and tenant-rights attorneys, senior centers, home-care agencies and hospital discharge planners white-label or refer.
problem: In regulated housing, a family member who can prove co-residency (typically 2 years, or 1 for seniors and the disabled) can succeed to the lease. The lease can be worth six figures over time. Landlords, who gain by re-renting at market, often contest, and the outcome hinges on documents families never assembled while the elder was alive (IDs, tax returns, bills, benefit and medical mail). After death the family faces a notice in weeks, with the elder's records locked in an unopened estate.
solution: Run a lease-inheritance readiness audit and an evidence ledger that collects only genuine documents (address-bearing IDs, filings, bank and medical mail, affidavits from neighbors). After a death, generate a Day-1 succession packet: notice to the landlord, agency filings, and attorney referral. Contested cases go to partner lawyers on contingency or through right-to-counsel programs.
why_now: NYC's political shift toward tenant protection, the SF rent emergency and record middle-income rent distress raise the stakes. The first Boomer tenants are aging out. Good Cause protections and local rent laws expand the leases worth inheriting. AI-generated pleadings are flooding housing courts, which raises the value of clean, verifiable evidence.
revenue_model: $199-399 per family file plus $6-9 per month for the evidence ledger. White-label and per-file fees from law firms, nonprofits and home-care agencies. Referral fees from partner attorneys.
non_obvious_insight: For many urban middle-class families the biggest asset passed at death is not money but a below-market lease, and the value is lost through missing paperwork, not through the law. The $124T wealth-transfer statistics ignore it entirely.
first_30_days: With two elder-law attorneys, draft evidence checklists from the state rent-stabilization rules. Run three clinics at senior centers or tenant associations. Charge $199 for the first 20 pilot families and track landlord responses. Publish a plain-language Succession Readiness Score for tenants.

title: Payment-Slip Doctor for Foreign Residents
one_liner: A LINE service that lets a foreign resident photograph a Japanese payment slip or government letter and get a plain explanation, deadline, consequences and payment help in their own language.
customer: Japanese-language schools, vocational schools and universities with many foreign students, at about ¥300 per student per month. Later customers are municipal national-health-insurance departments paying for improved collection, employers of foreign staff, and rent-guarantee and property-management firms.
problem: Foreign residents paid on average only 63% of national health insurance premiums by the end of 2024, according to a survey of about 150 local governments. From around FY2027, unpaid premiums and pension contributions will be a ground to deny visa renewal or change of status. Yet at my counter, foreign customers regularly hand me a slip or official letter and ask what it means. The barcode on a konbini payment slip is void after the due date, so I have to refuse it. Then a worker who cannot get to the ward office in daytime faces an arrears spiral that may end in a denied visa. The government mails a notice in Japanese that looks like junk mail.
solution: Photograph the slip or letter. The service reads the barcode and text, identifies the document type such as national health insurance, resident tax, pension or traffic fine, and explains in Vietnamese, Nepali, Chinese, Burmese or Indonesian what it is, how much, when due, and the consequences of non-payment. It sets calendar reminders and links to pay by PayPay, bank app or konbini. If the slip is expired, it generates a reissue script and shows ward-office hours and the nearest late-opening branch. Anything ambiguous or legal is escalated to a partner administrative scrivener. Stickers with a QR code at konbini payment counters are the acquisition channel.
why_now: The 2026 system upgrades that will link municipal payment records to Immigration Services Agency data, plus the rule that unpaid premiums will block renewals from around 2027, make payment compliance a visa issue for hundreds of thousands of students and workers. The current government has made foreign-resident rule enforcement a political priority. Schools are already adding payment-tracking features to their student systems. Nobody has built the explanation layer, and translation apps do not decode payment slips or their deadlines.
revenue_model: Schools pay ¥300-500 per student per month. Municipalities pay per successful on-time payment or a share of recovered arrears. Employers pay per foreign employee per month. Property managers and guarantors pay per tenant. A small paid human-escalation tier costs the user ¥980 per case.
non_obvious_insight: The failure point is not language in general. It is a single document, the konbini payment slip, and a single hidden rule that its barcode dies on the due date. People miss it by a day and the consequence is a visa problem. The counter clerk sees this daily, so the demand is proven and concentrated. Because the buyer of the outcome is a school or municipality, the paying customer is not the end user.
first_30_days: Build the LINE OA with barcode decoding, OCR and slip-type rules for the five most common slips, and Vietnamese, Nepali and Chinese output reviewed by native speakers. Put QR stickers on the payment counters of my three stores. Pilot with two Osaka language schools, about 300 students, at ¥300 per student per month. Measure on-time payment before and after. Bring the results to one ward's national health insurance department. Partner with an administrative scrivener firm for the escalation tier.

title: The 40 Days: Postpartum Confinement Caregiver Guild
one_liner: A trained, insured, tradition-certified caregiver guild delivering the 26 to 42 day postpartum confinement (yuesao, sanhujori, cuarentena) to diaspora families whose grandmothers are far away.
customer: New parents in Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese, South Asian, Latino and Middle Eastern communities in dense metros, mostly mothers at 30 to 36 weeks. Secondary payers: extended-family gift funds and employers or health plans looking to reduce postpartum depression.
problem: Confinement care is widely practiced but supplied through informal agencies and word of mouth. A US yuesao runs about $200 to $400 a day for the standard 26 days, and a 42-day term adds roughly 60%. Quality, safety and worker protections vary widely, agencies rarely serve non-Chinese traditions, and parents without a grandmother nearby are left choosing between exhaustion and a gray-market caregiver.
solution: Build the guild rather than a marketplace. Recruit experienced caregivers and give them W-2 employment, insurance and background checks, plus training in safe sleep, lactation basics, infection control and postpartum warning signs with an escalation path to the family's OB or midwife. Certify them in specific traditions (menus, do's and don'ts) and match on language and tradition. Sell modular tiers: nights only, meals only, 14, 28 or 42 days. Add a plain-language guide for in-laws and partners.
why_now: Immigrant-heavy metros have a large unmet pool of families who want the ritual, and grandmothers are harder to bring over given tighter visa and travel rules. Employer-of-record and payroll tools make W-2 caregiver employment easy for a tiny company. Postpartum mental health is a rising priority for employers and health plans.
revenue_model: $5,500 to $12,000 per family per engagement, at about 30% to 35% gross margin after caregiver pay. Meals-only tier at $35 to $55 a day for faster revenue. Employer or plan subsidy of $1,000 to $2,000 per birth. A gift registry for extended family.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is the trusted caregiver, so the moat is a certified workforce (training, payroll, insurance, safety escalation), not a listing site. Confinement is also the same intervention American medicine now calls the fourth trimester, so obstetric practices can refer to it without endorsing folk claims, and it has been an informal cash market that has never been professionalized.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with a dense Chinese-American or Korean-American community such as the San Gabriel Valley, Flushing or the Bay Area. Recruit 8 experienced caregivers through WeChat groups and existing agencies. Write a three-day training and safety protocol with a postpartum nurse and lactation consultant. Sign 10 founding families with a service guarantee, and sell a meals-only tier to 50 families for faster revenue. Line up two OB practices or doulas for referrals, and set up employer-of-record payroll.

title: Claims Desk for Government-Paid Childcare
one_liner: A medical-billing-style revenue-cycle service that turns small providers' attendance sheets into clean subsidy and universal-program claims and advances the cash within 48 hours.
customer: Family child care homes and one-to-three-site centers in states and cities with subsidy or universal-care programs, such as NYC and New Mexico (the latter from memory).
problem: As governments become the payer (universal-care promises, 2026 tax credits, tighter CCDF rules), providers face attendance logs, eligibility recertification, claim rejections, 30-60 day payment delays and fraud audits. Margins are thin, payroll is about 70% of cost, and the average worker earns $33,140. Home providers, the fastest-growing segment at +4.3%, have no back office.
solution: Providers send attendance photos or export from Brightwheel, Procare or Kangarootime. The service validates against each program's rules, fixes errors, submits claims and chases denials. It then offers advances against verified claims, funded by a partner lender. A running library of each state's rejection codes drives the automation.
why_now: Subsidy-fraud scrutiny and attendance-verification demands rose sharply in winter 2025-26 (from memory, not verified in the brief). Universal or free-care programs are launching and the DCFSA and 45F expansions add spending. Payment-rule changes reward providers who can document cleanly.
revenue_model: 3-5% of collected subsidy revenue plus a 1.5-3% factoring fee on advances. Payroll-timing savings make it an easy sell.
non_obvious_insight: Healthcare RCM became a giant industry because the payer changed. Childcare is going through the same payer shift with no RCM industry yet. The moat is knowing each state's rejection codes and quirks, which a services-plus-software firm accumulates claim by claim.
first_30_days: Pick one state with slow, public-rule subsidy payments. Recruit 10 home providers via Facebook provider groups and the local CCR&R. Do the claims by hand with one ops hire and a spreadsheet at 4%. Log every rejection reason. Add advances through a small-business lender partner in month 2.

title: Reserve-Crew Backup Photographers for Wedding Day Emergencies
one_liner: A paid-standby bench of pre-vetted, style-matched backup photographers who can be dispatched within 2-3 hours, sold to solo photographers as a subscription and to wedding insurers as claims fulfillment.
customer: Solo and small-studio wedding photographers ($199-399/yr for a 'Continuity Guarantee' they can promise couples), plus wedding-insurance carriers and MGAs that cover vendor failure but cannot produce a person.
problem: Every solo photographer's nightmare is a sudden illness, crash or family emergency six hours before a wedding. The standard backup plan in contracts is 'a photographer friend', which fails in practice. On peak Saturdays (dates like 10/10/26) every competent local shooter is already booked, so the Facebook SOS post at 6am gets 40 sympathetic comments and zero style-matched, available humans. Whoever does show up has never seen the timeline, venue notes, family-formals list or the photographer's look. Wedding insurance reimburses money after the fact but cannot supply a competent human in three hours. It is a capacity-reservation problem, not an insurance problem.
solution: Members upload style samples plus a 'Continuity Pack' for each booked wedding (timeline, family list, venue and light notes, gallery drop link), all in one place. We maintain a regional bench of vetted shooters tagged by style (documentary, bright and airy, moody, film-look). Bench shooters are paid a small standby retainer (about $40) to hold peak dates, plus an activation fee ($500-900) paid by the member or the insurer. On activation, the pack is pushed to the understudy, a coordinator handles couple communication, and images are delivered under the member's brand. Members display a 'Continuity Guaranteed' badge, which becomes a booking-conversion asset.
why_now: Vendor-failure cover is now a standard add-on in wedding insurance, and 2026 contracts increasingly require a comparable replacement or a full refund, so the gap between reimbursing money and supplying a photographer is now visible and contractual. Weekend supply is squeezed onto peak dates, and a growing pool of freelance portrait, real-estate and second-shooter talent with open weekends can be organized cheaply through Stripe Connect and shared workspaces. Insurers are also under pressure to reduce claim severity in small commercial lines.
revenue_model: $99-399/yr member subscription (tiered by number of weddings), per-activation fee split with the bench shooter (we keep about 20%), and an insurer contract of a flat per-policy fee or per-claim fulfillment fee. Standby retainers are funded from the subscription pool, like airline reserve crews.
non_obvious_insight: Backup fails precisely on the dates it is needed, because scarcity is correlated. The free 'photographer friend' network evaporates on peak Saturdays. The only fix is paying for reserved capacity in advance, and once you do, you own the only reliable answer to the industry's most feared event.
first_30_days: Pick one metro. Sign 25 solo photographers as founding members at $99/yr and recruit 8 bench shooters (portrait, real-estate and second-shooter talent with open Saturdays). Build the Continuity Pack in Notion/Airtable plus a shared Google Drive. Run a fire drill: on a chosen Saturday, ping every member's pack and time how fast each is delivered to a bench shooter. Pitch two wedding-insurance MGAs on a 90-day claims-fulfillment pilot, and get a lawyer to check contractor and liability terms before the first live activation.

title: Night Season: After-Dark Programming for Heat-Struck Venues
one_liner: A turnkey production company that converts heat-crushed summer attendance at zoos, gardens and ballparks into ticketed after-dark shows, with heat-triggered scheduling, on revenue share.
customer: Zoos, botanical gardens, minor-league ballparks, county fairs and water parks in the Sun Belt and Southwest, whose summer midday attendance collapses in heat waves and who set 2027 programming budgets in Q4.
problem: Extreme heat kills midday visits and creates heat-illness liability, while venue infrastructure sits idle. Venues know night events work (winter light shows, adult zoo nights) but lack lantern, projection or lighting capex, production talent and a heat protocol. New heat rules for outdoor workers in California, Washington and Oregon, with a federal OSHA rule targeted for October 2027, also make midday staffing costlier.
solution: A 'Night Season' program run from June to September. Lantern trails, projection mapping, night-safari tours, film and music nights, with hours moved by a WBGT trigger and a documented heat-safety protocol. We supply the show kit (leased), lighting crew, ticketing setup and sponsors such as hospitals and utilities as 'heat-safe' partners. The venue supplies land and staff.
why_now: Summer 2026 was reported as the hottest US July on record, so 2027 budgets will assume it repeats. LED lantern and projection costs have fallen, and WBGT sensors are cheap. Entertainment production talent is underemployed after studio and game cuts. Venues want revenue that does not depend on midday gates.
revenue_model: 35-45% of ticket and F&B revenue with no fee to the venue, leased show kits, and sponsorships. Illustrative math: 40 nights x 1,000 guests x $22 is about $880K gross per venue-season.
non_obvious_insight: Heat does not kill demand for outdoor leisure. It moves it about eight hours later. What blocks venues is show capex and know-how. A documented WBGT-triggered schedule shift is also a heat-illness risk reduction that a venue's liability insurer may recognize, so the program can help offset its own cost.
first_30_days: Pitch 10 Sun Belt zoos and gardens during the Q4 planning window with a mock-up and a $99 founders-pass landing page at two venues to test pre-sales. Sign a lantern or projection vendor on revenue share. Run a small heat-shifted pilot weekend in Arizona this October, while evenings are warm.

title: Insurability-at-Close Escrow for Home Listings
one_liner: Listing agents pre-underwrite a house and price the cheapest retrofit fix before listing, so buyers stop discounting for 'uninsurable' uncertainty.
customer: Listing agents, brokerages and sellers in Florida, California and Colorado foothill markets, paying a fee at closing.
problem: Contracts collapse or reprice when buyers cannot get a bindable quote inside the contract window. Homes labeled uninsurable trade to cash buyers at a discount. Much of that discount is uncertainty about fixable issues (roof age, vents, tree clearance), not permanent risk.
solution: A pre-listing 'Insurability File'. Run 3-5 carrier and E&S quotes through a partner agency, then identify the 1-3 cheapest fixes and get contractor quotes. Hold the retrofit cost in escrow at close and give buyers a bindable-quote certificate valid through closing. The buyer gets certainty and the seller gets a closing.
why_now: Citizens has shrunk from about 936K to about 395K policies, so private binding is possible for many Florida homes again. Fannie and Freddie now accept ACV roof coverage (Mar 2026), which opens cheaper insurable paths. Colorado and California rules now credit mitigation.
revenue_model: $750-1,500 per listing at close, plus a 15-25% referral margin on retrofit work and placement commission through the partner agency.
non_obvious_insight: The 'uninsurable' discount is a mispriced-uncertainty premium, and certainty can be bought. Whoever holds the bindable quotes at listing time sets the price.
first_30_days: Pilot with 3 top-producing agents in one Colorado or Florida market. Take 10 stuck or repriced listings, build files by hand, and measure price recovery against comps. Then productize the file template.

title: Bulk Records-Request Refinery, Septic-First
one_liner: Build datasets that do not exist by filing thousands of automated public-records requests to county health departments, then reading the scans with vision models and selling address-level reports.
customer: Home inspectors, buyer's agents, title and closing attorneys, and mortgage lenders and insurers in septic- and well-heavy markets, who pay per address report or a monthly subscription. Later customers are insurers and lenders buying bulk address-level datasets.
problem: About one in five US homes runs on septic and millions rely on private wells. Permits, inspections, pump-outs, repair and abandonment records sit in more than 3,000 county and town health departments, in paper, scans and idiosyncratic portals. There is no national database. Buyers sign blind and face 15-50k USD failed-system replacements. Inspectors and agents make phone calls to find records, or skip the check.
solution: A records-request engine. It knows each state's open-records statute, fee categories and portal type. It bulk-files requests, tracks deadlines, and follows up. A vision-language pipeline reads handwritten and scanned forms, extracts fields (install date, tank size, drainfield type, repairs, failed inspections, well depth and tests) and geocodes them to parcels. Sell address-level reports for 39-99 USD, with a guarantee of retrieve or refund at first. Every answered request becomes a permanent proprietary data asset, so the data compounds. The same engine expands to other records with no national database: hydrant flow tests, fire inspections, certificates of occupancy, unpermitted-work flags, underground tanks and radon.
why_now: Vision-language models now read messy handwriting and scanned forms at fractions of a cent per page, which made this economically impossible until recently. Most jurisdictions have moved to online request portals, making bulk filing feasible without postage and paper. Agents can draft statute-specific requests and chase deadlines automatically. Home-inspection firms are looking for differentiated services in a slow transaction market.
revenue_model: Pay-per-address report (39-99 USD), inspector subscriptions (149-399 USD per month for unlimited lookups in their region), and enterprise data licenses to insurers and lenders. Later, sell the engine as a service to other data-hungry industries that need one specific municipal record type at national scale.
non_obvious_insight: Government data is not secret, just expensive to collect, and that friction is the moat. Every request is legal, cheap and repeatable, but nobody wants to make 3,000 of them by hand, so once you have, nobody can scrape or replicate your dataset from the web. Concierge fulfillment lets you get paid on day one before the automation exists, and every manual retrieval trains the pipeline.
first_30_days: Choose one state with a septic-heavy housing stock and a friendly open-records law (for example, a state where county health departments handle onsite wastewater, such as North Carolina). Check the state law for commercial-requester restrictions and fee schedules. Offer 20 local home inspectors a 75 USD 'we retrieve the septic record or refund you' service, fulfilled manually or semi-manually at first. Simultaneously file bulk requests to every county health department for historical records. Run the vision extraction pipeline on the first few thousand pages, and use the results to pitch a subscription to inspector networks and title companies.

title: Turnkey Six-Bed Care Homes for Nurse-Operators
one_liner: A licensing-and-operations platform that turns ordinary houses into small licensed residential care homes run by nurses and experienced aides.
customer: Nurses, CNAs and senior aides (including immigrant health workers) who want to own and run a home, plus small investors and families who own a suitable house.
problem: Insiders think the senior-housing gap ($275B, about 549k units by 2028) needs towers, REIT capital and 3-5 year development. Yet many states license 4-10 bed homes in normal single-family zoning. The barriers are licensing know-how, fire and ADA retrofits, staffing plans and a steady flow of admissions, not capital.
solution: A 90-day licensing sprint: zoning and state licensing packet, retrofit checklist, insurance, policies and procedures. Then staffing playbooks (1:3 to 1:6 ratios), charting, medication and compliance software, an admissions pipeline from hospital discharge planners who can't find beds, and financing partners (HELOC, sale-leaseback, small-investor pools). Start with states that have small-home license categories (for example Washington adult family homes, Arizona assisted-living homes and California small RCFEs).
why_now: Occupancy is at 90.1%, the highest since 2007. Inventory growth was 0.4% in Q1 2026, the lowest on record, and nothing new arrives before 2030. Hospital discharge teams are desperate for beds, and seniors hold a record $14.92T in home equity.
revenue_model: $6-12k onboarding fee per home, 5-8% management or software fee on revenue, and a placement fee from families where permitted. Later a captive group-purchasing and insurance program.
non_obvious_insight: Supply can appear in 6 months if the constraint is permission and playbooks, not concrete. One nurse-operator with a 5-bedroom house at $5-7k per resident per month can rival a mid-size facility's per-bed economics with no construction.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 prospective operators through nursing-school and CNA Facebook groups. Sell a $2,500 feasibility-and-licensing sprint, publish a 'how to license a six-bed home in [state]' guide as lead-gen, and line up one hospital discharge planner as a first referral source.

title: Pickleball Court Noise Pre-Clearance Reports
one_liner: Standardized acoustic siting reports and low-cost monitoring loggers that let HOAs, senior communities and parks approve or defend pickleball courts before neighbors sue.
customer: HOA and condo boards, management companies, 55+ and retirement communities adding courts, city parks departments, and hotels, gyms and churches that want courts. They pay $1,200-$3,500 per site, plus a monthly logger rental. Complainant attorneys are a secondary buyer.
problem: Pickleball's popping sound is a legal flashpoint. In February 2026 two homeowners in Parkside at Boca Trail (203 homes) sued to shut two courts. Testing found up to 73 dB against a 55 dB city nuisance threshold, about 900 pops per hour, and nearest homes only 67-72 feet away versus the 300-500 feet often recommended. The homeowners have spent over $50,000 in legal fees, and the HOA paid $3,800 for an acoustic study. A 2023 survey found only 30% of residents wanted the courts unchanged and 28% wanted them closed. Boards cannot get neutral, standard evidence.
solution: A 'Court Siting Certificate'. It uses a calibrated Class 2 sound-level meter and a fixed protocol (LAmax, LAeq and 1-4 kHz pop-band readings at property lines and the nearest homes), then models the results against that municipality's ordinance. We keep a database of local noise ordinances and hours rules for the fastest-growing pickleball markets. The report ranks mitigation options by dB reduction per dollar: USA Pickleball's Quiet Category paddles and balls, acoustic fencing, hours limits and court orientation. A signed, board-meeting-ready PDF follows. Boards can also rent solar-powered sound loggers at $99/month to produce a continuous dB record for disputes.
why_now: Pickleball searches are about 8.4M (+42%). Glimpse reports retirement homes 'rushing to add the sport' and $10 CPCs. Lawsuits are arriving in 2026, the Boca Raton case being the first of its kind in Palm Beach County, and boards are converting tennis courts (this HOA did so in 2021). Every new court adds exposure.
revenue_model: $1,200-$3,500 per pre-clearance report or dispute audit, $99/month logger rental with monthly compliance reports, and referral fees from acoustic-fence installers and quiet-equipment retailers. Later: annual retainers with HOA management companies covering 50+ communities.
non_obvious_insight: Boards are not really buying noise reduction. They are buying neutral evidence and a defensible process before the fight starts. The Boca Raton case shows the asymmetry: a $3,800 study against $50,000+ in resident legal fees, with a split community (https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/pickleball-noise-sparks-lawsuit-tony-123055657.html). Glimpse's trend data flags pickleball demand among seniors and retirement homes (https://meetglimpse.com/trends/). The popular advice articles offer 'acoustic fencing, sound barriers, landscaping, buffer zones' but no costs, standards or benchmarks (https://spinwavepickleball.com/a/blog/pickleball-noise). A published, comparable measurement standard becomes the reference document that lawyers, city staff and boards all cite.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: buy two Class 2 meters and write the measurement protocol and report template, and compile ordinances for Florida, Arizona, Texas, the Carolinas and California metros. Days 8-20: cold-email 200 HOA management firms and community managers with a $750 pilot audit offer, and publish a 'pickleball noise ordinance by city' page for SEO. Days 21-30: complete 5 audits, get one board to publicly cite the report, and sign an installer referral partnership.

title: Personalized Cancer Vaccines for Dogs
one_liner: Falling costs of tumor sequencing, neoantigen prediction and small-batch mRNA make a bespoke cancer vaccine per dog plausible; start with the sequencing and design report oncologists can order today.
customer: Veterinary oncologists and university teaching hospitals, and owners of dogs with newly diagnosed aggressive cancers (hemangiosarcoma, osteosarcoma, mast cell tumors, lymphoma).
problem: Owners of dogs with cancer are offered chemo, surgery or nothing. The briefing notes about 80% of dogs with lymphoma never get IV chemo, and only one oral option has recently arrived. Owners will pay for hope, but experimental individualized therapies are inaccessible, and existing genomic panels mainly match small-molecule drugs rather than designing a vaccine.
solution: Phase 1: tumor-normal sequencing, neoantigen ranking and a clinician report in about 10 days, sold to oncologists. Phase 2: under a vet-school client-owned-dog research protocol, produce an individualized mRNA vaccine through a small-batch CDMO, with regulatory strategy set with USDA veterinary biologics and FDA CVM.
why_now: Sequencing runs at a few hundred dollars per genome, open protein and neoantigen prediction tools are strong, small-batch mRNA manufacturing is contract-accessible, and human personalized-vaccine programs are running. Loyal's conditional-approval progress shows vet regulators will work with novel therapies.
revenue_model: $1.5-3K per sequencing report, $10-25K per vaccine research-protocol fee, and licensing of the genomic dataset to human-oncology developers.
non_obvious_insight: Dogs are an excellent human-cancer model: spontaneous tumors, shorter timelines, owner-funded and lighter regulatory burden than humans. The paid 'hope' market is outside insurance, and the tumor-normal dataset itself is a licensable asset.
first_30_days: Partner with one vet-school oncology service and a sequencing lab. Enroll the first 10 dogs for sequencing-only analysis at cost. Sign an MOU with a small-batch mRNA CDMO. Submit a research protocol and recruit through oncologist referrals and owner communities. Individualized therapy remains experimental, so set expectations accordingly.

title: Fresh-Fall Meteorite Alerts and Landowner Desk
one_liner: Turn satellite lightning-sensor fireball detections into strewn-field maps within an hour, then broker signed landowner access and sale terms for hunters and dealers who pay for a 24-hour head start.
customer: Serious meteorite hunters, dealers and collectors (a few thousand worldwide), with museums and labs as secondary buyers of fresh, uncontaminated samples.
problem: Value depends on freshness and documentation. A witnessed fall recovered before rain sells for many times the price per gram of desert finds, and in my recollection a Martian meteorite sold for about $5.3M at auction in 2025. Hunters race using scattered social posts and public bolide feeds that arrive late. Landowners own the meteorites in the US, so the hunter who lands the landowner's yes wins.
solution: A pipeline that ingests public geostationary lightning-mapper fireball detections, weather-radar falling-debris signatures and upper-air winds to publish a dark-flight strewn ellipse in minutes. It overlays parcel data and gives the desk a landowner script, a one-page finder-landowner split contract, and a provenance dossier (time, coordinates, radar and satellite evidence) that raises sale price. Paid subscribers get the alert first.
why_now: GOES-19 became the operational eastern US geostationary satellite in 2025, with lightning imagers now covering the Americas and, as I understand it, Europe and East Asia. Open radar data is on the cloud, and the collectibles market is at extremes (a $16.5M single card in Feb 2026). LLM pipelines make a two-person alerting desk feasible.
revenue_model: $15 per month for hunter alerts, a $49 event pass for high-value falls, and 10% of sale value on brokered recoveries. Dealers pay about $300 per month for a priority feed and the landowner contract kit.
non_obvious_insight: Detection is free public data. The scarce input is speed to a signed landowner agreement before rain and rivals arrive. The business is a contracts-and-logistics desk that happens to run on satellite data, and the provenance dossier is the price multiplier.
first_30_days: Script the public fireball feeds and backtest on 2021-2025 falls. Open a Discord with 200 hunters and 5 dealers, and pre-sell 30 annual passes at $99. Offer to run the next credible fall end to end using the contract template, taking a percentage only if material is recovered.

title: Convert Empty Thai Hotel Floors to Monthly Stays
one_liner: Take under-filled floors of mid-tier Thai hotels on revenue share and run them as furnished 30-90 day remote-worker wings, replacing lost Chinese group demand with sticky monthly stays.
customer: Owners of 80-300 room three- and four-star hotels in Bangkok, Phuket, Pattaya and Chiang Mai whose Chinese group volume collapsed. End users are remote workers, retirees and long-stay sports or wellness visitors.
problem: Thailand's 2025 arrivals fell 7.2% and sit 17% below 2019, with Chinese arrivals down 33.5%. Insiders wait for Chinese groups to return, but Chinese outbound is shifting to independent travellers who go farther and spend less on hotels. Empty floors bleed fixed costs, while nomads on 40+ visa schemes struggle to find reliable monthly stays.
solution: We take 20-40% of rooms and add a coworking corner, bonded fast internet, laundry, community events and monthly billing. Guests pay USD 650-1,100 per month including utilities, for a 30-day minimum. We market through nomad communities and groups and help with long-stay visa paperwork. The hotel keeps F&B upside.
why_now: The China demand collapse leaves stranded capacity. Thailand's long-stay Destination Thailand Visa exists for remote workers, and 40+ countries now offer nomad visas. Nomad information is now free (Nomads.com sells lifetime membership for USD 1), so operators win on product, not discovery.
revenue_model: A 20-30% management fee on room revenue or a fixed lease spread, plus ancillary revenue from SIMs, insurance and visa-service referrals.
non_obvious_insight: Hotels are optimised for nights while nomads buy months. A floor at 90% occupancy on monthly rates beats 35% occupancy at full nightly rates, and monthly guests do not pay 22-28% OTA commission.
first_30_days: Sign 2 hotels in Bangkok or Chiang Mai on a 60-day trial of 10 rooms each. Build a one-page site and post in nomad and expat groups. Target 15 monthly bookings, and record occupancy and revenue per available room against the hotel's nightly baseline.

title: Second-Opinion Price Check for Vet Estimates
one_liner: Upload a photo of a vet estimate and get a line-by-line price benchmark and a list of questions to ask your vet within 24 hours, from vet-tech reviewers, for $19-29.
customer: Pet owners facing $500+ estimates (about 95M US households own pets), plus pet insurers and employers as a later benefit channel and independent clinics as a fair-price badge buyer.
problem: Vet services inflation ran 5.5% YoY in April 2026, and household spending at vets rose almost 4x as fast as spending on pet food and treats (about 1%). BofA Global Research says veterinary pricing is rising faster than wages, so many households delay wellness visits, dentistry and diagnostics. 25-30% of US veterinary practices, and roughly 75% of specialty clinics, are now owned by corporations or private equity (AVMA 2024, cited by BofA), which can erode competition. Pet insurance uptake stays low, and younger and lower-income households are pulling back on pet spending. When an owner is holding an estimate for a sick animal, there is no neutral benchmark.
solution: A mobile-first upload flow. OCR reads the estimate, and licensed vet techs (not diagnosing, just reviewing) compare each line item to regional price ranges, flag bundled or optional items, note which items are typically deferrable versus urgent, and give a short script of questions for the clinic. Every review adds anonymized line-item prices to a growing regional price database, which becomes the moat. Later features are a 'fair-price verified' badge for independent clinics and a payment-plan and generic-drug price check.
why_now: The data now shows a sharp split: sticker prices climb while pet food and store spending stalls, meaning owners are squeezed specifically at the vet. Private-equity consolidation is a live news story, and owners can share estimate photos easily. Pet-insurance carriers face rising claim costs and have an incentive to fund price transparency.
revenue_model: $19-29 per review, $9/month for unlimited pet-family plan, B2B licenses to insurers and employers ($1-3 per covered pet per month), and clinic subscriptions for verified fair-price badges ($99-199/month per clinic).
non_obvious_insight: The pain is not that pet care costs money, it is information asymmetry at the moment of an estimate, and the same dynamic is what made medical-bill advocacy a business for humans. Vet inflation is running roughly 4x pet-food spending growth, and owners are already responding by deferring care rather than shopping around, so the demand is for a fast, trusted benchmark, not another directory. Evidence: BofA Institute, 'The price of pet parenting has gone off leash,' 18 May 2026 https://institute.bankofamerica.com/economic-insights/pet-ownership-costs.html and full PDF https://institute.bankofamerica.com/content/dam/economic-insights/pet-ownership-costs.pdf (vet inflation 5.5% YoY, vet spending growth about 4x pet-store, 25-30% of practices corporate or PE owned, 95M pet households, $158B spend, deferred care). Legal caveat: state veterinary practice acts restrict diagnosing without a client-patient relationship, so reviewers must stay in price and question-generation territory.
first_30_days: Hire two contract vet techs at an hourly rate. Launch a landing page and post in owner communities and Reddit pet-cost threads with 'send me your estimate and I'll benchmark it free' to collect the first 100 estimates. Build the price table by hand in a spreadsheet, then charge $19 from review number 30. Approach one pet-insurance MGA or employer-benefit broker with the first regional benchmark chart. Target 100 reviews and 30 paid by day 30.

title: Knowledge Trusts That Pay Heirs From AI Licensing
one_liner: A fiduciary licensing shop that records a retiring or terminally ill master practitioner's judgment, holds the rights in an estate-friendly trust, sells non-exclusive licenses to AI buyers, and pays royalties to the expert and later the heirs.
customer: Two payers. First, employers and trade associations with an irreplaceable expert aged 62-75 about to retire, who pay for a knowledge-capture sprint. Second, AI labs, vertical AI vendors and professional-training firms that license the corpus. Beneficiaries are the expert and heirs. Channel: estate attorneys and wealth managers, who want an heir-engagement hook (Cerulli says 89% of firms treat family meetings as essential).
problem: The scarcest input for AI is long-tail, high-stakes tacit judgment (how a 40-year surety underwriter smells a bad bond, how a master electrician diagnoses an odd fault). It sits in the heads of people near retirement or death. Hourly expert-gig marketplaces pay by the hour with no royalties. They rarely reach 65+ specialists, and nobody structures who owns the recordings, annotations or persona rights after death, so it all falls into probate limbo. Meanwhile 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs are about 19% below trend (Stanford) and have no path to learn from these people.
solution: 1) Structured elicitation: 30-40 hours of rubric-guided sessions (case walk-throughs, 'what would you do and why not that', annotated redacted real work). Junior apprentice-interviewers from the same field, meaning recent grads or displaced mid-career people, run them. They are paid and earn a verifiable co-credit. 2) Rights go into a knowledge trust drafted with the client's estate attorney: consent controls, approved-buyer list, sunset dates, and no voice, likeness or persona cloning unless explicitly opted in. 3) Non-exclusive licensing of the corpus to labs and enterprise vendors. Royalties go to the expert while alive and to heirs afterward.
why_now: Mercor's $10B valuation (Oct 2025) and reported ~$2B gross run-rate (Jun 2026, lower-tier source, verify) proved frontier labs pay heavily for expert judgment, while contractors complain about pay and lack of protection. Roughly 4M Americans turn 65 each year, and Cerulli projects $124T in transfers through 2048. Postmortem publicity and digital-replica laws are maturing (for example California's 70-year postmortem term). The junior hiring freeze creates a cheap, motivated interviewer pool.
revenue_model: Employer-funded capture sprints at $15-40K per expert (a succession-planning budget line). License revenue share, roughly 40% to expert/estate, 40% to us, 20% to an apprentice pool. Trust administration fee of about 1% of royalties per year. Optional per-client fee from advisors or attorneys who bundle it into estate plans.
non_obvious_insight: The estate, not the living person, is the natural licensor of a lifetime of judgment. Postmortem and IP rights live in probate, and royalty streams fit inheritance planning better than hourly gigs do. Retirees who would never take a gig will happily fund grandchildren with a legacy asset. The demand is a fixed-time resource (a retirement wave) that becomes unavailable once experts are gone.
first_30_days: Pick two narrow, lab-relevant, high-liability trades (for example construction surety adjusters and commercial roofing estimators). Recruit 8-10 retiring experts via trade-association newsletters and five friendly estate attorneys. Pitch each expert's employer a $20K 'retirement capture sprint' as the cash-generating wedge, with licensing rights reserved for the expert's trust. Hire 3 laid-off or junior domain grads as interviewers. Run two pilots. Send redacted sample corpora to 10 human-data teams and vertical AI startups to pre-sell licenses.
